summary: This unit teaches you to recognise, group and choose the materials used in fabrication and welding. You will learn the difference between ferrous metals, non-ferrous metals and non-metals, the main properties of materials, the types of carbon steel, cast iron, stainless steel and the common non-ferrous metals and plastics, simple workshop tests to identify an unknown metal, how corrosion happens and how to prevent it, basic heat treatment, the forms in which materials are supplied, and how to choose, store and handle them.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). Every job starts with a material: the steel for a gate, the aluminium for a ladder, the copper for a pipe, the plastic for a tank. A welder or fabricator must know what a material is, how it behaves, how to recognise it, and whether it suits the job, because the wrong material can crack, rust away, bend or fail.

In Jamaica, materials also have to stand up to heat, heavy rain, humidity and, along much of the coast, salt air. Choosing and protecting materials well is what makes a gate, a railing or a tank stand last.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and anyone who chooses, orders, stores or works with metals and plastics in a workshop.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Sort materials into ferrous metals, non-ferrous metals and non-metals, and explain what an alloy is.
Explain physical properties (density, melting point, conductivity, magnetism) and mechanical properties (strength, hardness, toughness, ductility, malleability, elasticity, brittleness).
Describe mild, medium- and high-carbon steel, cast iron, stainless and tool steels, aluminium, copper, brass, bronze, zinc, lead and tin: their properties and uses.
Describe thermoplastics, thermosets, rubber, timber, ceramics and composites and where they are used.
Use appearance, weight, magnet, file and spark tests, labels and colour codes to identify a metal safely.
Explain why steel rusts, why the sea makes it worse, what galvanic corrosion is, and how to protect metal.
Explain annealing, normalising, hardening, tempering and work hardening.
Name the common forms (plate, sheet, bar, angle, channel, hollow sections and others), describe their sizes, and write a clear order.
Choose a material for a job and give the reasons; store and handle materials safely and keep them identified.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on material groups, properties, steels and cast iron, non-ferrous metals, plastics, identification, corrosion, heat treatment, forms of supply, choosing and storing materials.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as tin, carbon, density, thermoset, nickel, composite, melting point, work hardening and SDS) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: identifying and sorting a set of unknown metal and plastic samples with simple tests, and surveying the Centre's steel store and filling in a material selection sheet for a fabrication job. The assessor watches safe use of the grinder, careful recording and safe handling in the store.

blocks.note: Many questions ask you to choose a material and give a reason. Always link the choice to a property: "stainless steel, because it resists corrosion in salt air" earns more than "stainless steel, because it is good".
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Engineering materials are first split into **metals** and **non-metals**. Metals are then split into **ferrous** metals, which contain mostly iron, and **non-ferrous** metals, which contain little or no iron. (Ferrous comes from the Latin word for iron; iron's chemical symbol is Fe.)

head: Group
What it means
Typical properties
Examples and uses
rows: Mild steel: gates, grilles, frames, sheet work
Cast iron: engine blocks, machine bases
Stainless steel: sinks, rails, food equipment
Do not rust (though they can corrode in other ways)
Most are poor conductors of heat and electricity
Many are light and resist corrosion
Plastics: PVC pipes, polyethylene tanks, nylon bushes

blocks.p: A **pure metal** is one element only, such as pure copper or pure aluminium. An **alloy** is a metal mixed with one or more other elements, to make it stronger, harder, easier to cast or machine, or better at resisting corrosion. Most metals used in engineering are alloys.

head: Alloy
Made from
Why
rows: Iron + a little carbon (plus small amounts of manganese and other elements)
Stronger than copper; easy to machine; looks good
Tin + other metals (traditionally lead; now often silver and copper)
Melts at a low temperature to join metals
Aluminium + small amounts of magnesium, silicon or other metals
Stronger than pure aluminium but still light

blocks.note: A composite is not an alloy. An alloy is melted together, so its elements are mixed right through. A **composite** is two or more different materials bonded together, each keeping its own form, such as glass fibres held in resin (fibreglass) or steel bars set in concrete.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A material's **properties** tell you how it behaves. **Physical properties** describe what the material is like without any force on it. **Mechanical properties** describe how it behaves when a load or force is put on it.

head: Property
What it means
Example
rows: How heavy a material is for its size (its mass for each unit of volume)
Aluminium is about one third as dense as steel, so it is used where weight matters
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid
Aluminium melts at about 660 °C; steel at about 1 400–1 500 °C
How well heat flows through it
Copper carries heat away very fast, so it needs a lot of heat to braze; stainless steel holds heat in and distorts more
How well electricity flows through it
Copper and aluminium are used for wires; plastics and rubber are insulators
How much it grows when heated and shrinks when it cools
The cause of welding distortion; aluminium expands about twice as much as steel
Whether a magnet is attracted to it
Iron and most steels are magnetic; aluminium, copper and brass are not
How well it resists rust and chemical attack
Stainless steel and aluminium resist corrosion; bare mild steel does not

head: Property
What it means
Example
rows: How much load it can carry before it breaks. **Tensile** strength resists pulling, **compressive** strength resists squeezing, **shear** strength resists sliding (as in a bolt)
A tow chain needs tensile strength; a column needs compressive strength
Resistance to scratching, wear and denting
A file, a drill, a chisel edge
The ability to take a sudden blow or shock without breaking
A hammer head, a tow hitch, a crane hook
Breaking suddenly with little or no bending; the opposite of toughness
Cast iron and glass snap rather than bend
The ability to be stretched, drawn out or bent without breaking
Copper and mild steel can be drawn into wire
The ability to be hammered, pressed or rolled into shape without cracking
Lead, copper and aluminium sheet; hot steel at the forge
Going back to the original shape once the load is taken off
A spring; a steel rule that springs back straight
Staying in the new shape after the load is taken off
Bending a mild steel bar in the vice
Resisting bending or stretching under load
Steel is about three times as stiff as aluminium for the same size

blocks.note: Hardness and toughness are not the same. A hardened file is very hard but brittle: drop it on concrete and it can snap. A mild steel bar is softer but tough: it bends rather than breaks.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Metal
Density (g/cm³, about)
Melting point (about)
Magnetic?
Notes
rows: Melts lower than steel, so it casts well
Stainless steel (common sink and rail grades)
Can be slightly magnetic where it has been bent
About one third the weight of steel
Excellent conductor of heat and electricity

blocks.p: Example: a sheet of steel 1 m × 1 m × 6 mm weighs about 47 kg; the same sheet in aluminium weighs about 16 kg.

blocks.h: Why a welder needs to know properties

ul: To choose the right material for the load and the conditions.

To choose the right process, filler metal and amount of heat: aluminium melts at a low temperature and shows no colour change before it melts; copper conducts heat away so fast that it needs much more heat.
To avoid cracking: high-carbon steel and cast iron are brittle and can crack when welded.
To control distortion: metals that expand more distort more.
To work safely: some metals and coatings give off poisonous fumes when heated.

sections.title: Iron, carbon steels, cast iron and heat treatment

blocks.p: **Steel** is iron with a small amount of **carbon**, up to about 2%, plus small amounts of manganese and other elements. Carbon has a big effect: **the more carbon, the harder and stronger the steel, but the less ductile, the more brittle, and the harder to weld**. Iron with more than about 2% carbon is **cast iron**.

head: Type
Carbon (about)
Properties
Typical uses
Welding
rows: Soft, ductile and tough; easy to cut, bend, drill and weld; cannot be hardened much by heating and quenching
Gates, grilles, burglar bars, frames, brackets, sheet work, structural sections
Easy with MMAW, MIG or gas
Stronger and harder; less ductile; can be hardened
Needs care; often preheated, as the procedure says
Can be made very hard; more brittle
Chisels, punches, files, springs, knives, cutting tools
Hard to weld; cracks easily; avoid unless there is a proper procedure
Hard and brittle; casts well into complex shapes; resists wear; damps vibration
Engine blocks, machine bases, pipe fittings, vice bodies
Difficult; special electrodes and preheat; cracks easily

blocks.note: Many gates and grilles called "wrought iron" in Jamaica are really mild steel, often with cast decorations. True wrought iron is only found on old work.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Hot-rolled** steel has a blue-black skin of **mill scale** and is the usual stock for fabrication. **Bright** (cold-drawn) steel is smooth and shiny, more accurate in size, and costs more; it is used where a good finish or an exact size is needed.
**Heat treatment** means heating and cooling a metal in a controlled way to change its properties. The right temperatures depend on the steel: follow the supplier's data and your instructor.

head: Process
How it is done
Result
rows: Heat to the right temperature (a red heat for steel), hold it there, then cool it very slowly, for example in the furnace or buried in dry ash
The softest, most ductile state; stresses removed; easier to cut and bend
Heat in the same way, then cool in still air
A finer, more even grain; stresses removed; a little harder and stronger than annealed
Heat medium- or high-carbon steel to a cherry-red heat, then cool it quickly (**quench**) in water or oil
Reheat hardened steel gently to a lower temperature (about 200–300 °C), shown by the colour of the oxide on a cleaned surface, then cool
Less brittle and tougher, a little less hard

blocks.p: **Mild steel hardly hardens** when it is quenched, because it has too little carbon. Medium- and high-carbon steels harden; that is also why they can crack when welded and cooled quickly.

Polish part of the hardened tool so you can see the colours run along it as you heat it gently, and quench when the right colour reaches the working edge. The figures are a guide: follow the supplier's chart and your instructor.

Bending, hammering or rolling a metal while it is cold makes it harder and stiffer, and in the end brittle enough to crack. This is **work hardening**. You see it when copper pipe is bent back and forth, or aluminium sheet is hammered. **Annealing** makes the metal soft again: copper is heated to a dull red and then cooled, either in air or by quenching in water.

blocks.note: Hot metal and quenching are dangerous: use tongs, wear gloves, safety glasses and a face shield, keep quenching oil covered and away from flames, and lower hot work into the liquid slowly. Mark anything still hot with soapstone.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Stainless steel contains at least about **10.5% chromium**. The chromium forms a thin, invisible oxide film on the surface that stops rust, and heals itself if it is scratched.

The common grades for sinks, rails and kitchen equipment also contain **nickel** (for example 18% chromium and 8% nickel, often called 18/8 or grade 304). This makes them tough, easy to form and **usually non-magnetic**, although they can become slightly magnetic where they have been bent or worked cold.
**Grade 316** also contains molybdenum and resists salt water better. It is the usual choice near the sea.
Some stainless steels (for example many knife blades) are magnetic, so a magnet alone does not prove that a metal is not stainless.
Stainless steel can still stain, especially by the sea, if it is left dirty or if bits of ordinary steel get onto it from shared brushes, grinding discs or dust. Keep separate tools for stainless.

head: Steel
Main added elements
Properties
Uses
rows: Stays hard even when hot from cutting
Drills, taps, lathe tools, saw blades
Very tough; gets harder where it is hammered
Sinks, rails, food and boat equipment

blocks.p: What the main alloying elements do: **chromium** gives corrosion resistance and hardness; **nickel** gives toughness and, in stainless, a non-magnetic steel; **manganese** gives strength and toughness; **molybdenum** gives strength when hot and resistance to sea water; **tungsten** and **vanadium** keep tools hard at high temperatures.

head: Metal
How to recognise it
Main properties
Uses
Points for the welder
rows: Light silver-grey; dull grey when oxidised; white powder where it corrodes
About one third the weight of steel
Resists corrosion: a thin oxide layer protects it
Weaker and less stiff than steel (alloys are stronger)
Windows and doors, ladders, boats, roofing sheets, pots
Melts at about 660 °C with no colour change, so it collapses suddenly
The oxide layer melts far higher than the metal and must be cleaned off
Never grind it on a wheel used for steel: it clogs the wheel
Reddish-brown; turns dark brown or green with age
Excellent conductor of electricity and heat
Wiring, busbars, water and gas pipes, heat exchangers
Carries heat away fast; usually brazed or soldered
Taps, valves, plumbing fittings, keys, hinges
Gives off zinc fume when heated
Reddish-gold to brown; darker than brass
Strong and hard-wearing; resists sea water
Bushes and bearings, boat fittings, propellers, statues
Joined by brazing or special welding processes; follow the procedure
Fume causes metal fume fever: remove the coating and use extraction
Dull grey; very heavy; soft enough to scratch with a fingernail
Car batteries, radiation shielding, old pipes and old paint
Never breathe its dust or fume; wash your hands; no eating or drinking where it is handled
Solder; a thin coating on steel cans (tinplate)

blocks.note: Old painted gates, grilles and railings may have **lead paint**. Before cutting, grinding or welding old painted steel, ask your instructor; remove the paint carefully from the work area with the right protection, and never burn it off in a closed space.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Plastics are made from chemicals, mostly from oil. They are light, resist corrosion and insulate against electricity and heat. There are two main kinds.

head: Kind
What happens when heated
Examples and uses
rows: Soften when heated and harden again when cooled, again and again; they can be reshaped, welded with hot air, and recycled
PVC: water and drain pipes, electrical conduit, cable insulation
Polyethylene (PE, HDPE): water tanks, bottles, pipes
Polycarbonate: clear roof sheets, machine guards
Set hard for good when first heated or cured; cannot be softened again; they char and burn if overheated
Polyester resin: fibreglass boats and tanks

head: Material
Properties
Uses
rows: Very elastic; seals well; absorbs shock; perishes in sun, heat and oil
Seals, gaskets, O-rings, hoses, tyres, anti-vibration mounts
Packing, patterns, handles, bench tops, formwork
Hard and brittle; stand very high temperatures; electrical insulators
Firebrick, grinding wheels, spark plug insulators, porcelain insulators, glass, tiles
Two or more materials bonded together, combining their properties
Fibreglass (glass fibre in resin): boats, tanks, roof sheets; reinforced concrete; carbon fibre

blocks.note: Black polyethylene water tanks on roofs and stands, PVC water pipes and fibreglass fishing boats are everywhere in Jamaica. All of them soften, melt or burn with heat: keep sparks, spatter and hot metal well away from them when you weld nearby.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Burning plastics and rubber give off thick, poisonous smoke. Burning PVC gives off an acid gas (hydrogen chloride). Never burn plastic waste and never weld through or next to plastic without protecting it.
Cutting and sanding fibreglass makes a dust that itches the skin and harms the lungs: wear a dust mask, gloves and long sleeves.
Resins, hardeners and adhesives can burn the skin and cause allergies. Read the **safety data sheet (SDS)** before use: it gives the hazards, the PPE, first aid, storage and what to do with a spill.

blocks.p: Different metals can look alike, especially when they are dirty or painted. If the wrong one is used, a job can fail: a high-carbon bar can crack when it is welded, and mild steel used in place of stainless steel on a boat will soon rust. Identify a material **before** you use it.

head: Test
How to do it
What it shows
rows: Look at the colour and surface (clean a small spot if needed)
Mild steel: dark grey with blue-black mill scale, or bright if cold-drawn
Galvanised steel: dull grey, often with a spangled (crystal-pattern) surface
Stainless steel: bright silver; no rust
Aluminium: light silver-grey; white powder where it corrodes
Copper: reddish; brass: yellow; bronze: reddish-gold to brown
Cast iron: dark grey, with a rough, sandy cast surface; a grainy grey broken face
Lift it and compare it with a piece of steel of about the same size
Aluminium feels about one third as heavy; lead feels much heavier
Touch a magnet on a clean spot
Sticks firmly: iron, mild and carbon steel, cast iron (ferrous)
Does not stick: aluminium, copper, brass, bronze, lead, zinc and the common stainless steels
Sticks weakly: a common stainless steel where it has been bent or worked cold
Try an old file on a corner or an edge
Cuts easily: a soft metal, such as mild steel, aluminium, copper or brass
Cuts with difficulty: medium- or high-carbon steel
Touch a bare ferrous sample lightly on a grinder and watch the sparks
The colour, length and bursts of the sparks show the type of steel or iron (see the table below)
Cut a small chip from an edge
Mild steel gives a smooth curling chip; cast iron breaks into small crumbly chips

head: Material
What the sparks look like
rows: Long, straw-yellow streamers with few forks or bursts
Like mild steel, but with more forked bursts
Shorter, bright white streamers with many bushy, star-like bursts
Short, dull red-orange streamers with small, fine bursts
Shorter, orange to straw-coloured streamers with few bursts
Dull red, broken streamers with few bursts

blocks.p: Sparks are easier to judge in a dim place against a dark background. Compare the unknown with samples of known steels, ground the same way.

flow: Check the grinder: guard on, eye shield in place, tool rest close to the wheel (no more than about 3 mm gap), wheel not cracked
Wear safety glasses and a face shield; tie back hair and sleeves
Stand to one side while the grinder starts
Hold the sample with pliers if it is small, on the tool rest, and touch it lightly on the wheel
Watch the sparks; compare with known samples
Let the sample cool before you handle it; switch off and leave the area clean

blocks.note: Spark test **only bare ferrous metal** that a magnet has picked out. Never grind aluminium, copper, brass, galvanised steel or plastic on the bench grinder: soft metals clog the wheel and can make it break, zinc gives off poisonous fume, and plastic melts.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: The supplier's **label** or **certificate** (mill certificate) gives the exact grade of a bar, plate or sheet. Keep certificates on file for important jobs.
Many workshops and suppliers paint a **colour code** on the ends of bars, with a chart on the wall to show what each colour means. Codes differ between suppliers, so use your own workshop's chart.
Re-mark offcuts with their material and size before they go back on the rack.
Write the material used on the job card.
If a piece has no label and you are not sure what it is, test it or set it aside and ask your instructor. Never guess.

flow: Magnet test: magnetic pieces are ferrous; the rest are non-ferrous or non-metal
Non-ferrous: look at the colour and compare the weight
Ferrous: look at the surface, try the file, then spark test bare samples
Record every result on the record sheet as you go
Name each sample, or give the reason for the name you chose, and sort them into groups

blocks.p: **Rust** is iron oxide, the red-brown, flaky layer that forms when the iron in steel reacts with **oxygen and water**. Both must be there: steel kept dry hardly rusts. Rust is weak and porous, so it flakes away, lets more water in, and the steel gets thinner and weaker. It can carry on under paint that has been damaged.

**Salt** makes rust much worse. Salt water carries electric current far better than fresh water, which speeds up the chemical reaction. Along the Jamaican coast the air carries salt spray and is often damp, so bare steel near the sea can rust in weeks, and a poor paint job can fail in a year or two. Heat, humidity and heavy rain add to it.

ul: **Aluminium** forms a thin, tight oxide layer that protects it. In salt air it can pit and grow a white powder, but it does not rust away like steel.
**Copper** and bronze slowly turn brown and then green on the surface.
**Zinc** corrodes slowly, and protects the steel under it by corroding first.
**Stainless steel** is protected by its chromium oxide film, but can stain or pit in salt air if it is dirty or contaminated with ordinary steel.

blocks.p: When **two different metals touch** in the presence of water (especially salt water), they form a small battery, and one of them corrodes much faster than it would on its own. This is **galvanic corrosion**. In this list, when two metals touch, the one nearer the start corrodes:

head: Example
What happens
How to prevent it
rows: Aluminium roof sheets fixed with copper or brass
The aluminium corrodes round the fixings
Use suitable fixings with insulating washers
Galvanised pipe joined straight to copper pipe
The zinc, then the steel, corrodes at the joint
Use an insulating (dielectric) fitting or the right adaptor
Stainless steel bolts in an aluminium boat fitting
The aluminium corrodes round each bolt
Insulating sleeves and washers, or a sealant between the metals

blocks.p: To prevent it: avoid putting different metals together in wet places; where you must, **separate them** with plastic or rubber washers, sleeves, tape or paint, and keep the joint dry.

head: Method
How it protects
Points to remember
rows: Paint system: primer and top coats
Keeps water and oxygen off the surface
Clean to bare metal; remove slag and spatter from welds
Prime soon after cleaning, before rust returns
Near the sea, use a good primer and more than one top coat
Paint full of zinc dust that protects like galvanising
Used on welds in galvanised work and for repairs
The steel is dipped in molten zinc, giving a thick coating inside and out; the zinc corrodes first, so even a scratch stays protected
Long life outdoors and near the sea
Grind the coating off the weld area and use fume extraction before welding
A plastic powder baked on in a factory oven
A tough, neat finish for gates and rails; rust can creep under it where it is damaged
For bolts, screws and small parts
A film that keeps water off
For tools, machined surfaces and stored bar; it does not last
Stainless steel, aluminium, bronze or plastic
Costs more, but needs less upkeep
No places for water to sit
Drain holes, sealed or galvanised hollow sections, no gaps where water and dirt collect

blocks.note: For gates, grilles and rails near the coast, most shops use galvanised steel with the welds cleaned and painted with zinc-rich primer and top coats, or stainless steel where the customer can pay for it. Whatever is used, tell the customer to wash off salt and touch up chips.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Forms of supply, choosing and storing materials

head: Form
What it is
How its size is written
Example
rows: Flat and thick (often taken as about 3 mm and over; the dividing line varies)
Flat and thin; sometimes given as a gauge number
Depth × flange width (and mass per metre)
I-beam and H-beam (universal beam and column)
Hollow sections (RHS, SHS, CHS) and tube
Nominal size and wall (schedule), or outside diameter × wall
Plate with a raised pattern for grip
Thickness × width × length (check whether the thickness includes the raised pattern)
Sheet slit and stretched, or welded wire
Mesh size, strand size and sheet size

blocks.p: When you order, give the **material** (and finish, such as galvanised or primed), the **form**, the **size in the right order with units**, the **length** and the **quantity**. Example: "Mild steel SHS, 25 × 25 × 1.6 mm, 6 m lengths, quantity 8."

Steel in Jamaica comes from several countries, and many suppliers still use inches, feet and gauge numbers. Convert carefully and check the drawing: an inch size is often close to, but not the same as, the metric size.

blocks.note: Gauge numbers run backwards: the higher the number, the thinner the sheet. Gauges are not the same for galvanised sheet, aluminium and tube, so measure with a vernier caliper when it matters.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Ask: what must the part do, and where will it be? Then weigh up:

ul: **The load:** strength, toughness, stiffness.
**The conditions:** sea air, rain, chemicals, heat, sunlight.
**Weight:** must it be carried or moved?
**Making it:** can it be cut, bent and welded with the equipment you have?
**Appearance**, **cost** and **availability**, and how much upkeep the customer will do.

head: Job
A good choice
Why
rows: Strong, cheap, easy to cut and weld
Stainless steel (grade 316), or galvanised steel well painted
A ladder that must be carried
A cold chisel or a punch
A bush for a slow-turning shaft

ul: Store bars, sections and tubes on **racks off the floor**, sorted by material and size and labelled, so they stay dry and are easy to find.
Store sheet and plate **flat or on edge in a rack**, so they do not bend, with sharp edges protected.
Keep **stainless steel and aluminium apart from mild steel**, and use separate brushes and grinding discs: steel dust leaves rust spots on stainless steel and spoils aluminium welds.
Keep the store **dry and covered**: rain and sea air rust steel quickly.
Keep heavy items low on the racks; never climb the racks.
Keep plastics and rubber out of sunlight and away from heat.
Keep chemicals, paints and resins in their labelled containers with their **SDS** available.

Handling: wear gloves against sharp edges and safety boots; lift with your legs; get help or a lifting aid for heavy or long pieces; carry long bars with a person at each end; keep walkways clear and put offcuts back in the right rack.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can sort materials into ferrous metals, non-ferrous metals and non-metals, with examples and uses.
I can explain what an alloy is and name the metals in brass, bronze and stainless steel.
I can explain the difference between physical and mechanical properties, with examples of each.
I can explain strength, hardness, toughness, brittleness, ductility, malleability and elasticity.
I can give the carbon content, properties and uses of mild, medium- and high-carbon steel and cast iron.
I can describe stainless steel, tool steels and the common non-ferrous metals, with their uses.
I can tell thermoplastics from thermosets and name rubber, ceramics and composites with their uses.
I can identify a metal with appearance, weight, magnet, file and spark tests, safely.
I can explain why steel rusts, why the sea makes it worse, and what galvanic corrosion is.
I can describe ways to protect steel, and how to deal with galvanised steel when welding.
I can explain annealing, normalising, hardening, tempering and work hardening.
I can name the forms of supply, write their sizes in the right order and write a clear order.
I can convert common inch sizes and gauges to millimetres.
I can choose a material for a job and give the reasons.
I can store, label and handle materials safely.

c1.title: Sorting the offcut bin in Morant Bay
c1.text: At a training centre in Morant Bay, St Thomas, Tevin and Kayla are sorting a bin of unlabelled offcuts before the scrap dealer comes. They find: (A) a dull grey strip that is very heavy for its size and soft enough to mark with a fingernail; (B) a bright silver bar that a magnet does not attract; (C) a dark grey lump broken off an old machine base, with a grainy grey broken face; and (D) a length of steel tube with a dull grey, spangled coating.

c2.title: A fish market canopy at Alligator Pond
c2.text: A fishermen's co-operative at Alligator Pond, Manchester, wants a new steel frame for the canopy over its fish-cleaning tables, about 30 m from the sea. The old frame, made five years ago from bare mild steel square tube with one coat of gloss paint, is badly rusted, worst at the welded joints and at the feet, where water stands after rain. The new frame will be galvanised tube, welded on site, with aluminium roof sheets. The co-operative also wants stainless steel tables.

c3.title: A farm trailer near Santa Cruz
c3.text: Javier is repairing and extending a farm trailer for a farmer near Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. The frame is mild steel channel, the axle is a medium-carbon steel bar, and the leaf springs are high-carbon spring steel. The farmer wants a new tow hitch bracket welded to the frame. Javier's helper suggests cutting it from an old leaf spring, "because spring steel is stronger".

c4.title: Ordering steel for window grilles in Bog Walk
c4.text: Stacy-Ann is ordering steel for a set of window grilles at a small shop in Bog Walk, St Catherine. The drawing calls for 25 × 25 × 1.6 SHS, 12 mm square bar and 40 × 40 × 5 angle, all in mild steel. The supplier's price list gives "1 in × 1 in 16 ga square tube", "1/2 in square bar" and "1-1/2 in × 1-1/2 in × 3/16 in angle", all in 20 ft lengths.

c5.title: A chisel and a copper pipe near Highgate
c5.text: Leroy has a small farm workshop near Highgate, St Mary. He is making a cold chisel from a length of high-carbon steel bar. He is also bending soft copper pipe for a water line to his chicken house; after several bends and straightenings, one bend in the copper has become stiff and has started to crack.

questions.q: What is strip A most likely to be, and how should they handle it?
o: Aluminium: it is safe to grind it to show the bright metal
Zinc: heat it gently with the torch to see if it melts
Tin: put it with the steel, since tin is mostly iron
Lead: use gloves, do not grind or heat it, wash hands
questions.why: Lead is dull grey, very heavy and soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. It is poisonous, so its dust and fume must never be breathed, and hands are washed after handling it.

questions.q: Bar B is not attracted by a magnet. Which check best tells whether it is stainless steel or aluminium?
o: Try the magnet again on the other end of the bar
Compare its weight with a steel bar of the same size
Spark test it on the bench grinder and watch the colour
Look for red rust anywhere along its surface
questions.why: Both can be bright and non-magnetic, and neither rusts, so the magnet and a rust check do not separate them. Aluminium is about one third the weight of stainless steel; and aluminium must never be ground on the bench grinder.

questions.q: They spark test lump C. Which sparks would show that it is cast iron?
o: Long, straw-yellow streamers with very few bursts
Bright white streamers with many star-like bursts
Short, dull red-orange streamers with fine bursts
No sparks at all, since cast iron is non-ferrous
questions.why: Cast iron gives short, dull red-orange sparks with small fine bursts. Long straw streamers mean mild steel, and bright bushy bursts mean high-carbon steel. Cast iron is ferrous, so a magnet picks it out first.

questions.q: What is the spangled coating on tube D, and what must they not do with it?
o: Zinc from galvanising: keep it off the bench grinder
Chrome plating: spark test it to find the grade of steel
Aluminium paint: burn it off with the torch in the bay
Mill scale: wire brush it off to see the steel under it
questions.why: A dull grey, crystal-patterned (spangled) surface is a galvanised zinc coating. Grinding or heating it gives off zinc fume, which causes metal fume fever, and the zinc clogs the wheel.

questions.q: Why did the old frame rust worst at the welded joints and at the feet?
o: Paint was thin on the rough welds; water sat at the feet
Welding makes the steel near the joints lose its magnetism
The feet are lowest, so the salt air never reached them
Salt air attacks only the parts of a frame that carry load
questions.why: Paint does not cover slag, spatter and rough weld surfaces well, and water standing at the feet keeps them wet. With salt in the air, these are the places where rust starts first.

questions.q: The new galvanised frame is welded on site. What should be done at each joint?
o: Weld over the zinc, since it adds extra metal to the joint, then paint
Grind off the zinc, weld with extraction, then use zinc-rich primer
Weld over the zinc and leave the joint bare so new zinc can form
Burn the zinc off with the torch in the canopy, then weld the joint
questions.why: Zinc must be removed from the weld area, with fume extraction, to avoid zinc fume and porosity. Welding burns the zinc off, so the joint is cleaned and protected with zinc-rich primer and top coats.

questions.q: How should the aluminium roof sheets be fixed to the steel frame?
o: With copper nails, since copper never rusts in sea air
Straight onto the bare steel, so the two metals bond
With insulating washers or strips between the metals
With brass bolts, since yellow metals suit aluminium
questions.why: Different metals touching in damp, salty air cause galvanic corrosion, and aluminium suffers badly next to copper and brass. Insulating washers and strips keep the metals apart.

questions.q: Which stainless steel is usually recommended for tables so close to the sea?
o: Grade 304, the usual kitchen sink grade
A magnetic grade, as these are stronger
Any grade, as stainless steel never stains
Grade 316, which contains molybdenum
questions.why: Grade 316 contains molybdenum, which helps it resist salt water. Even stainless steel can stain or pit by the sea if it is left dirty, so it should be washed down regularly.

questions.q: Why is an old leaf spring a poor choice for the welded hitch bracket?
o: Spring steel is non-ferrous, so it will not weld to the frame
High-carbon steel is hard to weld and can crack near the weld
Spring steel is too soft to take the pull of the trailer
Spring steel rusts much faster than the mild steel frame
questions.why: High-carbon steel hardens when it cools quickly after welding, so the weld and the steel beside it can become brittle and crack. Mild steel plate of the right size is strong enough and welds easily.

questions.q: The frame is cut, drilled, bent and welded. Which property makes mild steel channel suitable?
o: It is very hard and resists wear
It does not rust in the open air
It is ductile and easy to weld
It is about as light as aluminium
questions.why: Mild steel's low carbon makes it ductile and tough, so it bends without cracking, cuts and drills easily, and welds without special procedures. It does rust, so it must be painted.

questions.q: The hitch takes sudden jerks when the tractor pulls away. Which property matters most for the bracket?
o: Hardness
Toughness
Malleability
Conductivity
questions.why: Toughness is the ability to take a sudden blow or shock without breaking. A hard but brittle bracket could snap under a jerk.

questions.q: Compared with the mild steel frame, the medium-carbon axle is:
o: softer and easier to bend cold
lighter, and not attracted by a magnet
as brittle as cast iron and hard to machine
stronger and harder, but less easy to weld
questions.why: More carbon makes steel stronger and harder but less ductile, and more likely to crack when welded. It is still magnetic and still machinable.

questions.q: About how long is each 20 ft length in metres?
o: About 2.0 m
About 6.1 m
About 7.6 m
About 5.1 m
questions.why: 1 ft = 304.8 mm, so 20 ft = 20 × 0.3048 ≈ 6.1 m. Plan the cutting list on 6 m lengths.

questions.q: The 1/2 in square bar is 12.7 mm, not the 12 mm on the drawing. What should Stacy-Ann do?
o: Check with her supervisor that 12.7 mm will suit before ordering
Order it anyway, since all square bar is really the same size
Order 1/4 in bar instead, as it is closer to 12 mm than 1/2 in
Order nothing and wait until a metric supplier has some in stock
questions.why: A change of size can affect the fit, the spacing of the bars and the weight. The supervisor or customer decides whether the nearest inch size is acceptable. 1/4 in is only about 6.4 mm.

questions.q: How should Stacy-Ann write the angle on her order so that there is no mistake?
o: Angle iron, 40 mm size, 3 lengths, the usual kind
40 × 5 mild steel angle, enough lengths for the grille job
Mild steel angle 40 × 40 × 5, 6 m long, 3 lengths
3 lengths of angle, the same size as the last order we placed
questions.why: A clear order gives the material, the form, the size in the right order (leg × leg × thickness) with units, the length and the quantity, so the supplier cannot misread it.

questions.q: Why has the copper pipe become stiff and started to crack?
o: Bending it cold work-hardened it; annealing will soften it
The copper has rusted inside, which makes it weak and stiff
Copper is a ferrous metal, so it hardens like steel when bent
The sun has overheated the pipe and turned it into brass
questions.why: Bending a metal cold again and again makes it harder and in the end brittle: work hardening. Heating copper to a dull red and cooling it (annealing) makes it soft again.

questions.q: Leroy hardened the chisel tip by heating it cherry red and quenching it in water. It is now very hard but chips easily. What should he do next?
o: Heat it red and let it cool slowly in ash to soften it
Quench it again in oil to make the edge harder still
Grind away the chipped edge and use it just as it is
Reheat it gently until it turns purple, then quench it
questions.why: Tempering makes hardened steel tougher and less brittle. For a cold chisel the edge is usually tempered to about a purple colour (around 270–280 °C). Heating it red and cooling it slowly would anneal it and make it soft.

questions.q: Leroy tries the same hardening on a piece of mild steel. Why does it hardly harden?
o: Mild steel contains no iron, so heat has no effect
It has too little carbon to harden when quenched
It must be quenched in oil, never in plain water
It must be heated until it melts before quenching
questions.why: Steel needs enough carbon (roughly 0.3% or more) to harden when quenched. Mild steel, with about 0.1–0.3%, stays fairly soft, which is one reason it is easy to weld.

questions.q: A black polyethylene water tank stands 1 m from a tank stand you must weld at a house in Seaforth, St Thomas. Why must it be moved or shielded first?
o: It is a thermoset that becomes harder and then cracks in the heat
Polyethylene conducts the welding current and can give a shock
A thermoplastic: heat and spatter melt it and can set it alight
The water inside the tank makes the welding arc spit and wander
questions.why: Polyethylene is a thermoplastic: it softens and melts with heat and burns with thick, poisonous smoke. Move it, or cover it with a fire-resistant blanket, and keep a fire watch.

questions.q: Overhead power lines are usually aluminium, often with a steel core, rather than copper. Why?
o: Aluminium conducts electricity better than copper does
Aluminium conducts well and is much lighter and cheaper
Aluminium is magnetic, which helps the current flow along
Copper rusts quickly when it is left in the open air
questions.why: Copper is the better conductor, but for the same current an aluminium conductor weighs about half as much and costs less, which matters over long spans between poles. The steel core adds strength.
